paragraphs.text: The teachings of the holy Scriptures are many and varied, but one grace shines on them all, and one source of teaching is the Spirit of truth. Whatever the Law prescribes, whatever the prophets teach, whatever the apostles proclaim, whatever the gospel of godliness dictates, all of it flows as from one abundant and fruitful spring, the Holy Spirit. No one can say anything worthy, think anything right or do anything wonderful unless the Holy Spirit confirms what is said, thought and done. For even if someone prides himself on human wisdom and has fortified his soul with human reasonings, if he shakes off the word of God he is nothing and will be counted as nothing. That is why the prophet says: "They have rejected the word of the Lord. What wisdom is in them?" For us, then, the Scriptures of godliness are the flowers of truth. The flowers are many, but one meadow nourishes them. The lamps of teaching are many, but there is one true luminary. The stars are many, but one heaven bears them. The branches are many, but there is one root. The fingers are many, but one hand writes with them. The strings are many, but there is one lyre of the Spirit. The teachings are many, but there is one source of godliness. Yet I marvel at this blind man. He had not read the Law, had not gone through the prophets, had never come upon the Gospels and had not been confirmed by the apostles, and still he called on the Savior of the world, saying, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me." Where did you learn to call him this, when you had not learned who it was you were calling on? You read no books, since you had lost your sight. You had no leisure for lessons, since you had only one occupation in life, asking, or rather begging. How then did you know the luminary of the world, whom you had seen neither in heaven nor on earth, since you were deprived of sight? But truly in him was fulfilled what David said: "The Lord makes the blind wise." A great crowd was around Jesus. The blind man did not know the luminary of truth, yet he perceived its working, and by the disposition of his heart he seized what his sight had not received. "What," he says, "does the crowd mean?" They tell him, "Jesus of Nazareth is passing by." What a marvel! He is taught one thing and proclaims another. He hears "Jesus of Nazareth," yet he does not call him "Jesus of Nazareth" but "Jesus, Son of David." Those who could see said what they supposed, but the blind man proclaimed what was true: "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me." So let each of you make this cry your own. Let a confession burst from your heart, and let each of you say this cry for yourself: "Son of David, have mercy on me." Brothers, when many people go to a house of mourning and see a body laid out and wept over by its family, they all weep. Some share in the grief, while others are going over their own troubles. Often a woman weeps and laments, yet not for the one laid out, since he is a stranger to her, but for her own who died before. Another's occasion becomes a reminder of her own sorrows. In the same way, brothers, when each of you hears what the saints proclaim, make the words your own and say for your own wounds, "Son of David, have mercy on me." Let each of you say it even now, roused by your own ills: one because he is blind in mind, another because his soul is deaf, another because his reasoning is lame, another because his will is leprous. For the afflictions that Christ healed in bodies occur in souls as well, and they need help from above. There is a blind soul that needs to recover its sight. The soul that does not see the wonders of the Law is blind. The soul that does not perceive the age to come is blind. The soul that sees the body of Christ but does not recognize his Godhead is blind. Isaiah testifies that the soul ignorant of the things of God is blind when he says: "And the servants of God were blinded." How were they blinded? "For you have seen many times," he says, "and have not taken heed; your ears are open, and you did not hear. And who is blind but my servants? And who is deaf but those who rule over them?" And the Savior, wishing to show blindness of mind, rebukes the Pharisees, who were blind to the truth, saying: "Let them be; they are blind guides of the blind. And if a blind man guides a blind man, both will fall into a pit." The deaf soul is the one that does not obey the Law and sets aside the Master's voice. It is deaf not by nature but by choice. That is why the Savior said: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." It was not that some of those present had no ears. How could they have attended to his teaching without the organ of hearing? Rather, he shows clearly that the visible ear was made for hearing, while the soul's perception is not tuned to hear the divine Law. So outward hearing is of no use when the inner mind has gone deaf. A leper in soul is not one whose body is discolored but one whose soul is darkened. For what is leprosy in the body but a double color? And what is leprosy in the soul? Double-mindedness. "Woe to the sinner who walks on two paths." When someone sometimes believes and sometimes disbelieves, sometimes leans toward almsgiving and sometimes toward inhumanity, he is leprous in soul. He has no healthy color but is divided in mind. As leprosy divides the body, so wicked reasoning divides the mind. So let each of you cry out for your own wounds and call on Jesus, the physician of souls and bodies, as the blind man cried, "Son of David, have mercy on me." Those who went ahead rebuked him, but those who tried to stop him did not hinder his boldness. Faith knows how to fight against everything and conquer everything. People rebuked him, yet the believer does not shrink back but follows the Master, knowing that shamelessness for the sake of godliness is a fine thing.

For if many are shameless for the sake of money, is it not best to put on this fine shamelessness for the salvation of the soul? Jesus commands that he be brought. The voice of one who called on him in faith made the Lord Jesus stand still. The man had already drawn near to him by faith, and now Jesus commanded that he be brought to him and come near in body as well. He commanded that he be brought, and says: "What do you want me to do for you?" He does not ask idly. He could have sent healing to him even as he sat there. But the Jews, who slandered the truth, could then have said, as they did of the man blind from birth, "It is not he, but someone like him." So he calls the man who is to be helped into the middle of a theater of ungrateful people, first to show the defect of nature and then to make known the authority of grace. "What do you want me to do for you?" He asks the man, but he teaches those present. And the man says, "Lord, let me receive my sight." See how many pledges he takes from the one receiving the cure, to shut out the slander of the wicked! Then he says: "Go; your faith has saved you." Do you see how what we said yesterday is shown by the deeds themselves? His benefits are not for sale, yet they are sold for faith. Jesus does not give his benefits for silver, but he sells them for faith. If you do not pay down faith, you do not receive the benefit. Grace is spread out, but faith must go first. There is one spring, but people draw from it, some with small vessels and others with larger ones. One draws a little water and another much, not because the spring apportions the measures, but because each draws according to his own vessel. In the same way grace is spread out like a spring, and the intention of the one who approaches becomes the vessel and container of grace. If you bring little faith, like a small vessel, you draw little grace; but if you bring a great mind, you draw a great benefit. That is why the Savior says, "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" The man answers, "Yes, Lord," and the Savior says, "Let it be done to you according to your faith." Hence the apostle urges the Corinthians, "Open yourselves wide," to show that a wider grace enters a mind that is widened. And the prophet says: "Open your mouth, and I will fill it." The hindrance lies not in the benefit but in our own sloth. Jesus has risen as the luminary of righteousness, and the ray of the spiritual sun is spread everywhere. One person enjoys less grace and another more, not because grace apportions it but because the mind sets the measure. There is one sun for the whole earth, one ray and one radiance, yet the whole world is not lit equally. One place has bright light and another dimmer, one more and another less, one a narrow beam and another a broader one. This is not because the sun gives more to this house and less to that one. The ray finds room according to the windows the builders opened, and so it pours in. In the same way, since our thoughts are the windows of our soul, when you open your thoughts wider you receive a wider benefit, and when you narrow your mind you narrow the grace. Unveil your thinking so that you may receive the radiance. That is why Paul says of himself: "And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed from glory to glory." One blind man was healed in the story, and the eyes of many are opened through the teaching. "Let it be done to you according to your faith." "And the blind man," it says, "followed him, glorifying God"; and Jesus does not stop him. Here we must consider the time when he healed the demoniac. The man who had received the benefit begged to follow Jesus, for "he wanted," it says, "to follow." But the Savior stops him and says: "Go to your house and declare how much God has done for you." Why does he stop the one who wanted to follow but not stop the other? Why does he allow this man to follow but not that one? It was useful for the one and beneficial for the other. He did not allow the first to follow for a particular reason: the man had been possessed, and a demoniac's speech and tongue are distorted. So he sends him out as a herald, so that his restored composure might proclaim his benefactor. It was a strange sight to see a man who had once been out of his mind now proclaiming sound words. So he makes the very organ of the man who was helped the herald of the one who saved him. And see the wonder: see the humility of the Savior, and see the gratitude of the demoniac. The Savior says: "Go and declare how much God has done for you." He does not say, "how much I have done for you," but in humility he puts it down to the name of God. But the demoniac went about proclaiming how much Jesus, who is God, had done for him. So he sends the one man out to proclaim, so that his restored state might show the greatness of the benefit, but he allows the blind man to follow. Why? Because he was going up to Jerusalem to accomplish the great mystery and to take on the dispensation for the world. The cross was to follow, and insult, and all the new outrages devised by those who fought against God. That is why he has the blind man follow: so that they might keep the memory of the miracle fresh, and so that the memory of the healing might steady the minds of those who were about to slip. He has the blind man follow so that no one might deny the miracle. For the minds of the apostles were to be tossed as in a storm, and the composure of those who watched was to be storm-beaten when they saw the Only-begotten of God on the cross. So that they might not falter when they looked on the passion, he allows the blind man to follow, so that with the memory of the benefit fresh they might keep their grasp of the truth unshaken.

Christ does many such things, since he came to take on the dispensation for humankind. So that no one might suppose that he suffered out of weakness rather than endured out of love for humankind, he looks at a fig tree before he enters Jerusalem. "And he went," it says, "looking for fruit on it, and found none." When he found none, he rebuked it, saying: "May no fruit ever come from you again." What sin had the fig tree committed? Does it bear fruit by the power of reason? Does it not put forth its fruit when the Creator wills? Besides, it was not even the season for figs, as the gospel testifies. What ordinary person, let alone God, demands fruit out of season? Creator, did you not fix the seasons? Did you not give seasons and times for bearing fruit? Why then do you demand fruit outside the season you yourself appointed? And even if it had been the season for figs and the fig tree had borne no fruit, would that have been a charge against its nature? Does it bring forth fruit whenever it wishes? Does it not produce its fruit when it is commanded? Why then does he rebuke the fig tree? Because he was about to undergo the passion, and so that they would not think he suffered out of weakness, he displays his power on a lifeless thing. He shows that he could have withered all who opposed him and destroyed all who fought against God. But since he came not to judge the world but to save it, as he himself said, he displays his power on the lifeless tree and keeps his love for humankind in store for human beings. So too here he allowed the blind man to follow, so that a fresh memory might remove the stumbling block and they might have the miracle shining before them. But another miracle followed this one. After the blind man recovered his sight, another man who was blind in soul recovered his. Who was this? The chief tax collector, blind where money was concerned, whose soul had been blinded by greed. For nothing blinds the soul so much as money. That is why Moses says: "For gifts blind the eyes of men and corrupt just words." The chief tax collector came, and Jesus was passing by: he who dissolves every sin, who destroys all wickedness, who changes darkness into light and makes crooked things straight. Zacchaeus was small in stature but great in longing, short in body but great in spirit. He was trying to see Jesus but could not because he was short. So he ran ahead and made up by contrivance for what his height lacked: he climbed a sycamore and watched Jesus pass by. But our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom Paul says that he "is able to do far more abundantly than all we ask or think," gave him not just as much as he longed for but more than he expected. Zacchaeus longed only to see him, but Jesus also honored him by becoming his guest. The one who had seen his mind says to him (for he knew his mind before Zacchaeus climbed the fig tree): "Zacchaeus, hurry and come down." The Savior is a fine fowler, bringing a soul down from a tree. "Zacchaeus, hurry and come down." He stretched out to him the reed of the word, smeared it with the birdlime of love, caught him by the wings of his mind and gathers him into his own church. See what he does. So that you will not think the word was forcing him, but will understand that the word of God is like a fowler, the blessed Zechariah says: "And the Lord showed me a fowler's vessel and said to me: I will not pass by my people until I have limed them." So it is an attested truth that the word of God is birdlime, entangling souls with love as with lime. Just as that glue no longer lets what it holds be separated from what holds it, so the souls united to the Savior are fastened as if by the fowler's glue. That is why David, a fine fledgling who had been caught, said: "My soul has clung close behind you." And again the apostle says: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him." He limes Zacchaeus, brings him down from the tree and brings himself into his dwelling. Zacchaeus had once darkened that house with his sins, but today the luminary of godliness has filled it with light. So when the Savior entered, the tax collector welcomed him with joy. Oh, the great goodness of the Master! The sinless one is with sinners, the fount of righteousness with the very stuff of unrighteousness, for greed is the stuff of unrighteousness. He entered the tax collector's house without being defiled by the darkness of greed; instead he destroyed the greed with the radiance of righteousness. And see the wonder. At once Zacchaeus stood at the doorway and said: "Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor." You have not yet been taught, and already you obey? You have not yet learned, and already you have kept the commandment? The Savior said nothing and taught nothing. He gave no counsel about almsgiving and did not then prescribe love for the poor. He was silent and quietly shed his light. The sun pours its rays into a house and lights it not by words but by its very working. In the same way the Savior, on entering, drove out the course of unrighteousness with the rays of righteousness. "For the light shines in the darkness," as the evangelist says. "Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor." He does well to divide his greed and cut his injustice in two. "Half of my possessions." Everything that is whole is strong, but once it is cut it is weak. "Half of my possessions." What fine words, overcoming nature, or rather overcoming habit, for habit is second nature! He banished his insatiable desire and recognized the truth. "Half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have wronged or defrauded anyone of anything, I pay it back fourfold." Here we must pay careful attention. Zacchaeus' wealth did not come from injustice alone but also from his father's estate. If it had all come from injustice, how could he have paid back fourfold what he took? And why does he say, "If I have wronged anyone of anything, I pay it back fourfold"? Though he had lived in lawlessness, he still knew the Law, and the Law commands a thief to repay what he stole fourfold. "If anyone steals a sheep," it says, "and is found out, let him repay four sheep." God makes the punishment fourfold, or rather the penalty, so that even if the Law does not frighten people, the penalty may shame them. For many who often have no respect for the law do respect a penalty. So he condemns himself. He does not wait for the verdict of the Law but becomes a law to himself, "for the law is not laid down for the righteous." The Savior welcomes these words and says: "Today salvation has come to this house." Zacchaeus justified himself, not merely because he saw Christ, but because he obeyed Christ's laws. "Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham." Before he did the works of Abraham, Jesus does not call him a son of Abraham but calls him simply by the name Zacchaeus. But once he had fulfilled the works of the patriarch by promising to care for the poor and renouncing injustice, Jesus says: "He too is a son of Abraham."

So we too, brothers, though we are Christians and are called Christians, are shown to be Christians by nothing so much as by the works of truth. Let us not, then, disgrace the name by our deeds, but let us adorn our faith with our deeds. We have been called sons of Abraham through faith; let us be called sons of Abraham through good works as well. For, as I said before, what is required is not noble bodily descent but likeness of conduct. That is why Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and all the patriarchs disowned the synagogue: its people did not inherit the faith of their fathers. Abraham disowned his own kin, because they did not follow his faith; Isaac and Jacob and all the patriarchs disowned them too. For whoever has denied God is denied even by kinship. And what text will bear witness that Abraham disowned the Jews? I ask so that we may not seem to be gloating over enemies, but rebuking those who have sinned. The blessed Jeremiah says, speaking for the people: "Lord, have mercy on us; the mountain and the city that our fathers blessed has been burned with fire. You, Lord, have mercy on us, for Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not acknowledge us. You, Lord, spare us." He means: since those we took pride in have become strangers to us and have disowned our race, have mercy on us, you whose love for mankind surpasses all. "Have mercy on us, for Abraham did not know us." For if he had counted our cause as his own, would he not have interceded for his own children? He interceded for the people of Sodom and was heard; would he not have been heard when interceding for his own? "Abraham did not know us." Abraham disowns those who are strangers to him in conduct, but, as I said, he claims as his own those who are strangers to his race but kin to him in piety. That is why Scripture, wishing to show the Jews that people take the name of those whose ways they choose, says: "Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite; your sister is a Sodomite." See how he builds kinship out of conduct. Because she thought as the Sodomites did, she was called sister of Sodom and daughter of the Canaanites. In this way he showed that he was not justifying anyone by race but honoring character. But I think even the Canaanite and the Amorite disown the kinship. When the Canaanite sees those who fight against God and are strangers to piety coming over to him, he disowns them and will not accept being called father of the ungodly. Why does he disown them? If you assign them to the Canaanite [?] and say, "Your father is a Canaanite," he too will say: "Is this my son, who has denied the faith of his fathers? I am not faithless, even if I am a Canaanite. The Canaanite woman will bear witness to my faith, crying out: Son of David, have mercy on me." So let them not be called sons of the Canaanites, for they did not keep the faith of the Canaanite woman. Let them be called sons of stones and wood, those who say to a stone, "You are my father," and to a piece of wood, "You gave birth to me." But I think even the stones disown them, and the wood renounces kinship with the faithless. A stone too can disown them and say: "The son of ungodliness is no child of mine; the son of injustice is no child of mine. For though I am a stone, I have heard Scripture say: God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham." "Very well," someone says, "you are speaking for the stone, but does a stone talk?" Listen to the prophet, who says that a stone will cry these things out from the wall, and a beetle in the woodwork will speak. And: "Even if you are silent, the stones will cry out." What then shall the race of the faithless be called? They are not sons of Abraham. They are not Canaanites either, because of the Canaanite woman, for the brightness of her faith put their unbelief in the shade. Nor are they sons of stones, for even the stones disown the kinship. What name is there for the faithless? Jeremiah gave them a name: "Call them rejected silver, for the Lord has rejected them." So let us be afraid too, brothers. Are you proud of your noble kinship with Christ? Then let Christ's righteous judgment make you afraid. Yesterday we preached about almsgiving: that everything must come second to almsgiving, and that the soul must be valued above all things. I have also been amazed at another piece of folly: people with no children take adopted sons, and one man adopts a father, another a brother. You adopt a stranger as your son, and you avoid the Master? Adopt the one who pays you back your reward; let Christ become your son. "That is a fearful thing to say," someone objects. "Watch what you are saying. Don't let a turn of phrase lead you away from reason and drag you into absurdity. You call Christ the son of a man?" But I call him not only son but also brother, and not on my own authority: I am following his own words. Someone once said to him: "Your mother and your brothers are looking for you." The Savior said: "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother and sister and mother." And if such a person is his mother, then he who honored righteousness with this title is the son of that mother. So let every soul become a mother of Christ in its disposition. How can it be a mother of Christ? Every soul is in labor with Christ within itself, but unless it is transformed by piety it cannot be called a mother of Christ. When you receive the word of Christ, shape it in your mind, and give it form in your thoughts as in a womb, you are called his mother. Each one of our souls, I mean, becomes a mother of the word of Christ, and Christ is formed in each one. To show you this, Paul says: "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." Have you done righteousness? You have formed Christ in your soul. Have you given alms? You have formed the imprint of truth. This does not mean that Christ himself is formed in each person. He calls the word of piety "Christ," because through it we take on the imprint of truth. Have you given alms? You have formed Christ. Have you done righteousness? The imprint of truth has been formed. So we must pay attention to how we ought to adopt Christ as a brother. Take him as a partner in your affairs. You do not want to give him everything? Then at least give him half, as Zacchaeus did. "But Zacchaeus gave to Christ himself," someone says, "not to the poor." Listen: "Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God." When you give to the poor, you have given to Christ. Do you not know that he takes what is given as given to himself? Do you not know what a fearful judgment he has set down for you in writing? He says: "When the Son of Man comes at the renewal of all things, he will set the sheep on his right and the goats on his left, and he will say to those on his right: Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you, for I was hungry and you gave me food."

See how he who borrows through the poor acknowledges the debt: "I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me." So outwardly you are clothing a naked man, but in truth you are clothing Christ. Clothe Christ, so that he may clothe you on the day of judgment. Shelter him, so that he may shelter you on the day of wrath. Listen to David saying: "He sheltered me in the hidden place of his tent." Shelter is needed. That fearful fire is coming, the Gehenna from which there is no reprieve, and if Christ's hand does not shelter you, the fire will recognize you as a stranger. It knows how to seize strangers and how to honor the saints. It respects piety and seizes ungodliness. There no wealth or money can win it over, no authority, no power. All stand on equal footing before the judgment seat of Christ. Even if there are differences among human beings, before the Master all are of equal rank, however great the difference. How great is the difference between an angel and a man? Great, and no small one. How great is the difference between the sun, the moon and the stars? Yet they are summoned together under the law of worship. How great is the difference between plants, angels and animals? Some are immortal, others mortal, yet each one, under the yoke of service, acknowledges its Master. That is why David joins in one harmony things set apart by rank, saying: "Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights; praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts; sun and moon." For though a thing is lower in rank, it is united with the rest in service. Brothers, it is like the ranks of honor in the world. They are distinct from one another, but they are united under the yoke of service. Everyone bows to the emperor, everyone trembles before his authority. The difference lies in the ranks; among the servants there is harmony. So it is there too: all people are equal, and the only ones who are not equal are those who surpass the rest and shine with piety. That is why Daniel rightly said: "I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like an Ancient of Days took his seat." Pay close attention here, I beg you, to how he portrays the Judge of truth as if in a bodily image. Since God is bodiless by nature, he draws spiritual things through things of the senses, as in a picture. So he says "like an Ancient of Days," not aged by time but honored for his eternity: "His clothing was white as snow, the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels a burning fire. A river of fire flowed before him; a thousand thousands stood before him, and ten thousand times ten thousand served him." O fearful tribunal! O memory enough to frighten the heedless! If these things are so fearful to hear, how much more fearful will they be to see? "And I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, books were opened, and thrones were set up." Whose thrones? Clearly those of the holy apostles, to whom the Savior said: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, you too will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." "Books were opened": books in which evil deeds are written and good deeds are written, books in which each person's life is recorded. He calls it a book not because God has parchment and letters, but because for you a book is a tool of memory, and so he portrays God's memory as a book. God has no need of a book: his memory is his book. We humans read the prophets, the apostles and the Gospels and cannot carry them in our hearts without a book, but that does not mean God needs one. The source of all memory needs no book. There virtuous deeds are written, and there evil deeds are written. Do not fear that the verdict is already settled. Even if your evil deeds are written down, they can be wiped out by good deeds. And the reverse is true: if someone's name is written down for his piety but he denies it by his conduct, having been written down does not settle his verdict, for the name is wiped out. A person written down for his piety can be wiped out and cast out for his negligence. To show you this, David says of the Jews who were once written down and afterward wiped out: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous." Just as the faithless are blotted out, so the faithful are written in. Listen to Paul: "Greet the brothers who are dear to us, and my yokefellow, with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life." Let us fear that book. Be afraid that your sins may be written down. Think how you feel before a judge, when the records against you are opened in front of a magistrate, exposing your injustice and publishing your madness. Think how much fear, how much trembling there is, how the limbs shake and everything inside churns, when a mere man is judging. If there is such fear when a man is judging, who can describe the fear of that day when the Master of all will judge the world? We say these things not to frighten you but to bring you to your senses. Let money not be preferred to Christ; let injustice and greed not be preferred to God. Did you hear what was said before, that prosperity lasts only as far as the grave? We went over this yesterday. Why wait for the grave to put an end to your way of life? Wait for the grave to be only the end of this life, so that through the present life you may be ferried across to the life to come. Love the works of righteousness. The grave is where we are dissolved, where the earthen vessel vanishes. Let us flee the judgment to come, brothers, I beg you. These things must be spoken with feeling and heard with feeling. Let us take up a longing for righteousness. See how the prophet cries out: "Woe is me for the day of the Lord, for the day of the Lord is near." If a prophet trembles at the thought of that day, shall we, who are answerable for countless sins, think of it without fear? Let us win over the Judge by repentance, let us wipe out our sins, let us fear that fearful voice which says: "Whoever denies me before men," and it is not the one who denies in word who truly denies, but the one who denies by his conduct, "I too will deny him before my Father. Whoever confesses me, I too will confess him before my Father." If the words are fearful when we examine them, will not the realities be far more fearful when we see them? Picture it, brother. The Judge of the world is seated. Angels stand beside him, archangels guard him, the cherubim glorify him, along with the powers beyond the world and the hosts beyond the heavens. Among all these are patriarchs, prophets, apostles, evangelists and martyrs, and the kings of this world, rulers, judges, potentates, rich and poor, ordinary people and wise, all of them standing before the judgment seat. And in front of so many witnesses in heaven and on earth, the Judge speaks and disowns the strangers before the Father: "For I will deny the one who denies me," he says, "before my Father."

Picture him saying: "Father, this man despised my faith, this man persecuted my own, this man insulted my Church, this man publicly vilified my own, this man spat on my word, this man trampled on my preaching." He says this not to inform a Father who does not know, but to expose the enemy publicly by the accusation. Picture the Judge speaking when he summons the glorious ones of the earth bound in manacles. For Scripture says: "to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles." Those on trial, the potentates, stand there in fear, and the Savior says: "These spat on my word of truth, these set aside my law, these annulled my teaching, these punished the apostles, these tortured the martyrs." He says these things; picture it. When the King speaks, how fearfully the angels standing by nod, how dreadfully they threaten, already consuming the sinner with their gaze! Picture the angels indignant, the archangels stirred, the powers shaken, the Father indignant, the Holy Spirit angered, and that man driven out in great shame. He is driven out not only from salvation but into condemnation. For the fearful thing is not only failing to be saved and to reign, but being handed over to the fire as well. "But whoever confesses me, I will confess him." Picture how great the glory, how great the boast, how great the crown, when the Judge says: "This man kept my word, this man preached my faith, this man confirmed my word, this man did not overlook my poor, this man trampled on greed and preferred righteousness, this man laughed at the world as if it did not exist and loved the world to come, this man carried my kingdom far and wide, this man honored my word. Honor him, Father." When we say these things, putting words in his mouth, we are not dividing the dignity of Father and Son or undoing their authority. The form of an accusation is used to show the Judge's indignation, and all these things serve for the salvation of those who confess and the condemnation of those who disbelieve. But the most fearful thing of all is this. Picture Michael and Gabriel and all the angelic hosts standing, while the sons of Zebedee are seated, Paul and Peter are seated, men drawn from humankind. The angels stand by in fear, and men sit in confidence. Picture the angels standing and the fishermen and tax collectors seated, and let us join them in saying: "How great is the abundance of your goodness, Lord!" Zacchaeus sits, Paul and Peter sit, and Michael stands by. We are not using strange names; we are keeping to what is written. We have not learned the names of angels from anywhere else; we are following the Scriptures. There is no envy there, no jealousy, for these are not earthly matters. The angels are not grieved that they stand while human beings sit, for they share in the glory of the saints. Hear the Lord saying: "Truly I tell you, there is joy in the presence of all the angels over one sinner who repents." So let us love the glory of Christ and spurn the glory that passes away like a dream. You were told yesterday how the prophet called the glory of the world a dream: "The wealth of the ungodly," he says, "will be like a dream." Our present condition is no different from a phantom. Yesterday in health, today in sickness; yesterday in power, today brought low; yesterday rich, today poor; yesterday proud, today despised. Everything is shaken, everything changes. And I do not mean human things only, for "heaven and earth," he says, "will pass away, but my words will not pass away." That is why those Christians are blessed who stay humble even in high office. Have you been humble in your high office? Then being humbled will do you no harm, for when it comes it will find you already as you ought to be. If you humble yourself before humiliation comes, it will bring nothing new against you; your mind is ready, and you are equipped for the battle. So David rightly said: "I was ready and was not troubled." Let us flee boasting, flee vainglory, and love Christ, and the poor for Christ's sake. Then he who enriches all and has mercy on all may grant the church a great multitude, so that it may flourish in piety and keep its husbandman of righteousness. He was absent yesterday because of other duties, but he is with us through his spiritual oversight. For our people are not like the Jews, that I should say they were like sheep without a shepherd. They are an apostolic people, with a shepherd after the Gospel's pattern who says: "Though I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see the firmness of your faith in Christ." To him be the glory and the power, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
